item.title: Security policy
item.description:
Reporting a vulnerability

Do not open a public issue or pull request for a security vulnerability.

Email security@circleci.com, whether the problem is in Smarter Workflows or in the CircleCI platform. CircleCI’s security team receives the report. The project sets no response target, and CircleCI has no bounty program (process).

For a sensitive report, encrypt the message with the key at https://circleci.com/.well-known/pgp-key.txt.

Include the steps to reproduce, the release or commit, and the planner version (circleci-smarter version).

Supported versions

Smarter Workflows is at version 0.x. Fixes land on main and ship in the next release. The code and the design have not been independently reviewed or penetration-tested.

Support

Smarter Workflows is a CircleCI Labs project. CircleCI support does not cover it, and field engineers handle bugs and feature requests on a best-effort basis, with no SLA. Use GitHub issues for problems that are not security vulnerabilities.

What the planner does with your credentials and your repository

Limitations lists the known gaps in detail.

  • The continuation key (CIRCLE_CONTINUATION_KEY) is read only by circleci-smarter continue. It never prints the key or the request body, only the status code.
  • A trace records the paths of the tracked files that a job read and the directories it listed, not their contents. The impact map is built from those paths.
  • The impact map lives in the project cache, and any branch can write a cache entry. A forged map could make the planner skip jobs. Mandatory jobs and the guardrails do not depend on the map, and every default branch run is a full run. Signing the map on the default branch is planned.
  • The guardrail bundle runs locally in the setup job, against the config that the planner generated. The same bundle can be enforced org-wide as a config policy.

item.title: 3. Build the impact map from file-access traces of full runs on the default branch
item.description:
Date: 2026-11-13. Status: accepted.

Context

Smarter Testing builds an impact map on the default branch, then uses it on other branches to pick the tests a change affects. This project wants the same loop for jobs:

  1. a full run on the default branch rebuilds the map;
  2. branches use it;
  3. a merge triggers the next full run, which rebuilds it again.

A job’s equivalent of test coverage is the set of repo files it reads. There are several ways to record that:

  • Hand-written globs go stale.
  • Language analyzers need one per ecosystem, and miss scripts and config files.
  • strace and LD_PRELOAD are slow, and Go binaries bypass libc.
  • fanotify and eBPF need privileges that Docker jobs do not have.
  • Access times (atime) cost nothing. Under the usual relatime mount option, the first read after a write always updates a file’s atime. A freshly checked-out file has atime equal to mtime, so a file that was read has atime greater than mtime.

Decision

  1. On full runs of the default branch, the planner adds two steps to every job of the pruned workflow:
    • Right after checkout, a reset step sets the atime of every tracked file and directory to the epoch, because checkout itself reads every file. It also probes that atime works on that filesystem.
    • A post-step records the tracked files and the directories whose atime has since moved past the epoch: the ones the job read or listed. A job whose filesystem fails the probe gets an incomplete trace.
  2. A final job merges the traces into the impact map.
  3. It saves the map to the project cache under a key derived from the commit SHA.
  4. On other branches, the planner restores the map for the merge-base commit, falling back to the newest map.
  5. Only green full runs produce a map.

Consequences

  • No ML, no per-language code, no hand-written globs. The map explains itself: “this job read these files”.
  • noatime filesystems, busybox find and non-Linux executors give incomplete traces, so those jobs always run.
  • Because a read is “atime past the epoch”, an input that is read and then rewritten in the same job (a formatter run with -w) still counts as read. Traces still miss inputs from outside the repo: see ADR 2 for how those are covered.
  • Cache entries can expire (default retention) and can be written by any branch. A missing map means a full run. Mandatory jobs and guardrails do not depend on the map. Signing the map on the default branch is planned hardening.

Verification (2026-11-13)

Tested on CircleCI’s docker executor (cimg/base, overlay, relatime) and machine executor (ubuntu-2404, ext4, relatime):

  • After the checkout step, 43 of 44 tracked files already had atime newer than mtime, because checkout reads them.
  • After the reset step, a job that ran cat README.md; ls docs was traced as exactly README.md and docs.

item.title: Backtest
item.description:
The backtest command replays historical CI runs against today’s impact map and reports how often select mode would still have run failing jobs (recall) and how much job time it would have skipped (savings).

Method

For each record in a history file, the planner runs in select mode with the recorded base, commit, branch, and changed paths. That reuses internal/planner exactly as plan --mode select does; backtest does not duplicate selection logic.

For each job that ran in CI:

Outcome Meaning
Caught The job failed and select mode would still run it.
Miss The job failed and select mode would skip it.
Unmatched The job failed but its name is not in today’s workflow (renamed or removed); excluded from recall.
Flaky The job failed then passed on a rerun of the same commit; excluded from recall.

Recall is caught / (caught + misses) over non-flaky failures in jobs that still exist in the config.

Savings sums duration_s over matched jobs that ran historically but would be skipped, divided by matched recorded job time. Unmatched job time is reported separately.

History file format

A JSON array of commits:

[
 {
 "commit": "sha",
 "base": "merge-base sha",
 "branch": "feature/x",
 "changed": [{ "path": "pkg/foo.go", "status": "M" }],
 "jobs": [
 { "name": "go-test", "status": "failed", "duration_s": 120.5 }
 ]
 }
]

Optional per-commit parameters overrides the --parameters file for that pipeline (same semantics as plan --parameters).

Build a history file with scripts/bench/fetch-history.sh (needs a CircleCI API token and a git clone). Fixture parsing is tested by scripts/bench/test-parse.sh.

Command 

circleci-smarter backtest \
 --history history.json \
 --map impact-map.json.gz \
 --config .circleci/continue.yml \
 --workflow ci \
 --parameters pipeline-params.json \
 --mandatory security-scan \
 --format md

--parameters is a JSON object of pipeline parameter values, applied to every commit unless a history record carries its own parameters object. Use the same file you would pass to plan --parameters when the continuation config gates workflows or jobs on << pipeline.parameters.* >>.

--format json writes the machine-readable report (used for golden tests).

Scheduled benchmark on main

The benchmark workflow in .circleci/continue.yml runs when pipeline.trigger.type is schedule (the schedule is configured on the project in CircleCI, not in this file). It uses the smarter-workflows-ai context so fetch-history.sh can call the API with << pipeline.project.slug >> (GitHub App projects use the circleci/org/project form). It restores the latest impact map cache, fetches the last 200 ci pipelines, runs backtest, and stores backtest.md and backtest.json as artifacts.

Limits of replay

  • One map for all commits. The map reflects the repo layout at its revision (usually recent main). Older commits that touched different paths or job names are approximate.
  • Changed files only. History carries a file list, not full git trees. Adds/deletes may miss directory moves the live planner would see via git ls-tree.
  • Workflow drift. Failures in jobs removed from the config or renamed are unmatched (listed separately, not in recall). Savings count only jobs present in today’s workflow.
  • Parameter gates. Without --parameters, workflow when expressions that depend on pipeline parameters may be unknown, which forces a full run and makes savings look like 0%.
  • No guardrail replay. Backtest does not pass --policy-bundle; historical guardrail repairs are not simulated.
  • Flaky detection depends on CircleCI job rerun metadata when history is mined; hand-written fixtures set "flaky": true explicitly.

Use backtest to compare maps and tuning over time, not as a guarantee for every past commit.

Measured: this repository (2026-11-15)

Replayed 79 commits from the project’s ci workflow against the impact map from main at commit 83d7d6082:

Metric Value
Failures (non-flaky) 5
Caught 5
Misses 0
Flaky (excluded) 0
Recall 100%
Historical job time 13 737 s
Would have skipped 949 s
Savings 6.9%

History here is mostly Go and .circleci/ changes, which reach most jobs, so skipped time stays small. Replaying the demo monorepo history would not measure much: those pipelines already ran in select mode when the traces were taken.

item.title: Limitations
item.description:
What v0.1 does not do yet. Each item is safe: where the planner cannot decide, the job runs.

  • One planned workflow. Other workflows in continue.yml pass through with the same meaning. YAML anchors, aliases and merge keys are expanded everywhere, and formatting such as indentation may change.
  • The gate is a no-op job, so it runs no steps and cannot check anything itself. It only passes when the jobs it requires pass. --gate-image no longer picks its image (the gate has none): it is a deprecated alias of --map-image, the image of the impact-map job.
  • Job groups are one opaque unit. An entry that names a group under job-groups always runs, with everything it requires, and is not traced. Its serial-group and the group are kept as written. The planner and layout check do not look inside a group: a restricted context used by a job inside one is not seen, and a job outside the group cannot require a job inside it.
  • A release job (type: release) is never traced. It stays when a job it requires runs, and then so does everything it requires.
  • Matrix jobs always run.
  • Orb jobs are traced only with --trace-orb-jobs: it adds a checkout and a reset as pre-steps, so it only suits orb jobs that check out the repo. Without it they always run.
  • A checkout inside a command gets no reset, so that job’s trace comes out incomplete and the job always runs.
  • Expression filters (string filters) are reported, and left out of the gate.
  • Workflow when/unless are evaluated only when every value is known from --parameters, --branch, --tag and --trigger-type. Unsupported forms still mean a full run. When the condition is false, the workflow is not pruned and gets no gate (CircleCI skips it).
  • A job that requires only filtered-out jobs by a status (- deploy: failed, with deploy filtered out on the branch) may or may not run, so the plan cannot leave it out or drop its requirement: it is a full run.
  • Inputs from outside the repo are not traced: the network, time, secrets, images. Full runs on the default branch, mandatory jobs and --extra-inputs cover them.
  • The impact map lives in the project cache. Any branch can write a cache entry, so a forged map could skip jobs. Mandatory jobs and guardrails do not depend on the map. Signing maps on the default branch is planned.
  • Setup job time. The plan job takes about a minute here, because it builds the planner from source. A released binary would make it a few seconds.
  • The report’s job count includes jobs that filters exclude on the branch.
  • Planned next:
    • history mining and learned rules;
    • an optional model decider (paths only by default);
    • compose mode (agentic);
    • Chunk sidecar integration (the same impact map, in the inner loop);
    • releases and a published orb.

item.title: 7. Impact map v2: shared path tables and compact indices
item.description:
Date: 2026-11-15. Status: accepted.

Context

Impact map v1 stores every repo path verbatim in each job’s files and dirs arrays. On large monorepos the JSON grows with the number of job×path pairs (roughly jobs × average reads), blows past the 16 MiB parse cap, and takes seconds to decode. A realistic shape is thousands of jobs each reading a large fraction of tens or hundreds of thousands of unique paths.

Decision

  1. On-disk format v2 (still JSON, gzip-compressed as impact-map.json.gz):
    • Sorted files and dirs tables: each repo path appears once.
    • Per job, file_idx and dir_idx are standard base64 blobs of sorted delta varints over table indices (first index absolute, later indices encode the gap from the previous one).
    • Metadata unchanged: revision, created_at, method, and per-job complete and nodes.
  2. Why delta varints instead of bitsets: Indices are dense when jobs read many files but sparse when they read few; delta varints are small in the common case, need no third-party format, and decode in one pass with strict bounds. Roaring or raw bitsets win when sets are extremely sparse across a huge table; this workload is usually “many indices per job out of a shared table”, where varints are simpler and fast enough.
  3. Writers (map build, the trace map job) emit v2 gzip only. Readers accept v1 JSON (legacy cache) and v2 gzip; plan tries impact-map.json.gz then impact-map.json.
  4. Caps (oversize or malformed → full run): compressed file ≤ 64 MiB; decompressed JSON ≤ 256 MiB; when compressed size < 64 KiB, decompressed must be ≤ 32× compressed (zip-bomb guard); ≤ 4096 jobs; ≤ 200_000 file table entries; ≤ 50_000 dir table entries; ≤ 100_000 indices per job per table; job names ≤ 256 chars. v1 maps keep the former 16 MiB uncompressed cap.

Consequences

  • Monorepo-sized maps fit in cache and decode in sub-second time on developer hardware (see docs/benchmarks-perf.md).
  • Path tables must stay sorted and deduplicated; corrupt index blobs fail closed at parse time.
  • Cache artifacts change extension; operators with only v1 files still work until the next default-branch map build.

Verification (2026-11-15)

go test ./internal/impactmap -run TestBenchMapV2FitsTarget on this branch: synthetic 2000 jobs × 10k files each, v2 gzip under 20 MiB and decode under 0.5 s.

item.title: Threat model (v0.1)
item.description:
Smarter Workflows runs inside a customer’s CircleCI project: a setup workflow plans which jobs to run on a branch, then continues the pipeline. This page is generic; it does not describe any one org’s policies.

Assets

  • Repository source — integrity and confidentiality as for any CI job.
  • Continuation config — defines the jobs that run after setup; may reference contexts and images.
  • Continuation key — secret that authorizes continuing the pipeline (environment variable).
  • Impact map — gzip JSON (v2) or legacy JSON (v1) in the project cache describing which files each job read on a past full run.
  • Plan report — plan.json / plan.md with job decisions and diffs.
  • Trace scripts — shell embedded in customer job configs (reset-atime.sh, collect-trace.sh).
  • Policy bundle — Rego guardrails evaluated before continuation.

Trust boundaries

Actor Trust Reaches
Default-branch full run Semi-trusted Writes traces and impact map to cache
Feature branch / fork PR Untrusted for map May restore a cache entry from any branch
Planner binary (setup job) Trusted by operator Reads map, config, git; writes continuation config
Trace collector (per job) Trusted code, hostile repo data Reads git checkout only; no network
CircleCI continuation API Trusted endpoint Receives key + config over HTTPS
Policy bundle on disk Trusted by operator Evaluated locally; no upload in v0.1

Threats and mitigations

Forged or hostile impact map

Threat: A branch writes a cache entry claiming jobs did not read files they actually use, so the planner skips work.

Mitigations: Mandatory jobs always run. Guardrails do not depend on the map. Unusable paths mark a job incomplete (it runs). Oversized or malformed maps are rejected (full run). v2 bounds compressed and decompressed bytes, table sizes, job count, and per-job index counts at parse time (v1 keeps a 16 MiB cap). See ADR 7.

Residual risk: A plausible forged map can still skip optional jobs until signing on the default branch (limitations). Operators should treat map cache as hint data, not proof.

Injection via config, map, or YAML emission

Threat: Job names, paths, or parameters break out of generated YAML or inlined shell.

Mitigations: Gate and map key prefixes match a safe identifier regex. Map job steps quote version and binary path for /bin/sh. Trace scripts are static literals (no customer interpolation). Embedded scripts avoid tabs and CircleCI template syntax. Job names with expressions trigger a full run.

Residual risk: Customer-authored job definitions in the catalog are unchanged; only added smarter steps are constrained.

Trace scripts in customer jobs

Threat: Malicious repo layout or environment breaks quoting, leaks secrets, fails the job, or exhausts resources.

Mitigations: set +e; always exit 0. No network. No printing environment variables. CIRCLE_JOB hashed for filenames; job text sanitized to one line in the TSV. Temp dirs under .git. GNU tool probes fail closed to “unsupported trace”. Hostile path tests in scripts/test-trace.sh.

Residual risk: Very large repos cost time during find/git traversal; tracing is only on the default branch by default.

Continuation client

Threat: Key or config leaks via logs, redirects, or error messages.

Mitigations: Errors name HTTP status only. Response body not logged. No redirect follow (key stays on intended host). HTTPS required except loopback. Config size capped at 8 MiB. Key redaction if ever present in an error string.

Residual risk: Operator misconfiguration (HTTP to a non-loopback host) is rejected at client construction.

Policy bundle loading

Threat: Symlink or path traversal loads Rego from outside the bundle directory.

Mitigations: Walk stays under bundle root; symlinks skipped; *_test.rego ignored. Hostile YAML in config fails Check without executing customer code.

Residual risk: Evaluated config is still customer YAML interpreted by circle-policy-agent; bundle should be operator-maintained.

CLI output paths

Threat: Odd --out / --report-dir values or world-readable continuation config.

Mitigations: Null-byte paths rejected. Continuation config written 0600; plan report files 0640 in a 0750 directory; impact map 0640.

Residual risk: Paths are absolute or relative as the operator gives them; the CLI does not sandbox writes outside the workspace.

Related docs

  • Limitations — forged map and other accepted gaps
  • How it works — data flow
  • Spec v0.1 — formats and algorithm

item.title: 4. The catalog is native CircleCI config
item.description:
Date: 2026-11-13. Status: accepted.

Context

The first idea was a new catalog.yml with metadata on each job. That is one more format to learn and keep in sync. The jobs, commands, executors and orbs a team uses already live in its CircleCI config, or in orbs it shares.

Decision

  • Select mode (v0.1): the catalog is the project’s own full continuation config (.circleci/continue.yml). The planner prunes those workflows and keeps the order, approvals, filters and contexts the team wrote.
  • Planner settings (mode, mandatory jobs, full-run paths, extra inputs) are parameters of the orb job, not a new file.
  • Shared catalogs are orbs, pinned to exact versions: the only job-level units that cannot change underneath you.
    • URL orbs are allowed only when pinned to a commit SHA.
    • CircleCI functions are step-level units, so they are building blocks for compose mode, not jobs.
  • Compose mode (later): an agent wires jobs from a catalog orb (jobs, commands, executors) into workflows, and the guardrails bound what it can produce.

Consequences

  • Adoption means moving the pipeline into continue.yml and adding one setup job. No new schema.
  • What the planner generates reads like the team’s own config, minus the skipped jobs, plus the gate job.

item.title: Validation
item.description:
What was tested in v0.1, and what each layer found. Unit, robustness, guardrail and trace results are from 2026-11-14; end-to-end and backtest numbers are from 2026-11-15.

Test layers

Layer What Result
Unit and golden planner, config, diff, impact map, report; 12 example scenarios with golden plans and configs; a fuzz target pass
Robustness 27 unusual config shapes (approvals mid-graph, two workflows, matrices, orb jobs, status requires, anchors and merge keys, null steps, renames, unicode paths). End-to-end scenarios

Twenty-one scenarios on two targets: the demo monorepo (16 scenarios, 13 jobs, select mode) and this repository (5 scenarios, 8 jobs). Each scenario ran three times on the same base commit (63 pipeline runs total). Every run checked the jobs that ran (besides smarter-gate), guardrail outcome where relevant, and the continued workflow’s GitHub check conclusion.

First batch (63 runs): 57 passed the job-set check. Six did not:

self-orb (×3) The change step edited orb/orb.yml, which no longer exists; the orb lives under orb/src/@orb.yml. The branch was never pushed.

Bugs that validation found and fixed

  • A job’s requires on a filtered-out job: the planner now follows CircleCI’s documented rule. A filtered-out requirement is ignored, unless every requirement is filtered out.

item.title: 5. A Go binary that is also a circleci CLI extension
item.description:
Date: 2026-11-13. Status: accepted.

Context

The tool has to be easy to adopt in production if product teams like it. The circleci CLI dispatches circleci <name> to a binary named circleci-<name>; Smarter Testing’s testsuite is one such extension. CircleCI’s policy engine is a public Go library (circle-policy-agent), so a Go binary can evaluate policies exactly the way the service does.

Decision

Ship a single static Go binary, circleci-smarter, that can be called directly or as circleci smarter. It embeds the trace collector script, and links circle-policy-agent for the pre-flight. The orb downloads a pinned, checksummed release. Until releases exist, it builds from source.

Consequences

  • One language and one binary, with no runtime dependencies in the planner job.
  • The trace collector stays a small POSIX shell script, so jobs need no extra binary.

item.title: 6. Every plan passes the guardrails before it continues: check, repair, or fall back
item.description:
Date: 2026-11-13. Status: accepted.

Context

CircleCI config policies also evaluate the continuation config. Server-side enforcement needs the Scale plan, and a continuation the server rejects fails the pipeline after the setup job has already spent its one continuation.

Decision

  1. The planner runs the project’s policy bundle locally, against the config it generated, using circle-policy-agent.
  2. Policies in the bundle tag violations the planner can fix with a machine-readable code, e.g. [smarter:require-job=security-scan]. The planner applies the fix and plans again, up to 3 times.
  3. A violation it cannot fix turns the plan into a full run, which is checked again.
  4. If even the full config fails, the setup job fails with the violations listed, without continuing.
  5. The same bundle can be pushed as org policy, limited to the projects that opt in, starting with soft-fail.

Consequences

  • Guardrails work on every plan, Scale or not. On Scale they are also enforced server-side.
  • Policies cannot read parameters as values, so the planner emits literal config and never adds parameters.
  • Compose mode will reuse the same loop, with an agent doing the repair.
